subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Climate Change and Coffee
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Climate Change and Coffee.

hook.text: By 2050, climate change may cut suitable Arabica-growing land in half. The world's favorite coffee is at risk.

buildup.text: Arabica needs stable temperatures between 18–22°C, consistent rain, and no frost. Even small changes hurt yields.

discovery.text: Farmers are moving plantations higher up mountains to chase cooler temperatures. But mountains have peaks.

twist.text: Some regions will gain—parts of China and East Africa may become new coffee frontiers as climates shift.

climax.text: Lower yields, higher costs, and shifting zones mean coffee prices will likely trend upward for decades.

punchline.text: Coffee doesn't adapt to heat. The climate crisis is a coffee crisis.

quiz.question: How much might suitable Arabica-growing land shrink by 2050?

details.summary: Rising temperatures, unpredictable rainfall, and increased pest pressure threaten to cut suitable arabica growing land by up to 50 percent by 2050. Farmers face declining yields and quality. Climate adaptation through heat-tolerant varieties and shade management is urgently needed.
details.whyItMatters: Climate change is an existential threat to the coffee industry. Without adaptation, the coffee we know and love may become scarce and unaffordable.
takeaways: Suitable arabica land could shrink 50 percent by 2050
Rising temperatures increase pest and disease pressure
Heat-tolerant varieties are being developed urgently

faq.question: How exactly does climate change affect coffee?
faq.answer: Higher temperatures stress arabica plants, reduce cherry quality, and expand the range of pests like the coffee borer beetle. Erratic rainfall disrupts flowering and harvesting cycles. Droughts reduce yields while heavy rains cause soil erosion and fungal diseases.

faq.question: What is being done to save coffee from climate change?
faq.answer: World Coffee Research is developing climate-resilient varieties. Farmers are planting shade trees, moving to higher altitudes, and adopting water conservation. Some research explores crossing arabica with robusta for heat tolerance while preserving flavor.
